summary:
Marswalk Planner is an in-browser EVA route planner for a human explorer at Jezero Crater, built on real NASA terrain, imagery and weather. Perseverance has already found the places worth sending a person to: the Three Forks sample depot, organic-bearing mudstones, the "leopard spots" of Cheyava Falls. Our app answers the practical question: can an astronaut walk there from the base, do the work and get home alive, given slopes, suit endurance, oxygen, daylight, comms and cold?

You place a base and science stops on the map. The app finds least-time routes on a 20 m terrain grid that avoid slopes beyond the suit limit and lean away from loose ground. It then gives a go / caution / no-go verdict on slope, suit endurance, daylight, oxygen, walk-back range, comms, shadow, temperature, ground and radiation. A reach map shows where you can walk, work and still get home in time over real terrain. An emergency-return check finds the worst moment of the walk for an injury or a leak. An auto planner fits the most science targets into one EVA. Every walk can be replayed in 2D and 3D, with live oxygen and Perseverance raw images at each stop.
details:
What it does

Marswalk Planner is a planning aid for a crewed walk (EVA) at Jezero Crater. You set the base and science stops. The app computes the route, checks it against suit and environment limits, and replays the walk. It runs entirely in the browser.

Live app: https://marswalk-planner-one.vercel.app

Source code (public, Apache 2.0): https://github.com/Magurin/marswalk-planner

Features

  • Terrain routing: least-time A* paths on a 20 m grid. Cells steeper than the suit limit (20° by default) are closed. Slopes near the limit and loose ground are penalized, so the route prefers a gentle detour.
  • Go / caution / no-go: checks for slope, suit endurance, daylight, oxygen (with a 45-minute reserve), walk-back range, line of sight to the base, shadow, air temperature, ground under foot, radiation, terrain coverage and emergency return. The overall verdict is the worst single check.
  • Reach map: where you can walk, work 30 minutes and still get home in time, computed over real terrain rather than in straight lines.
  • Emergency return: for every point of the route, the cost of turning back right then at half the pace and twice the oxygen use. The app shows the worst moment.
  • Auto planner: an exact Held-Karp search over up to 14 targets that finds the most science stops fitting in one EVA, in the best order.
  • Terrain analysis: slope classes sharpened by the 1 m HiRISE model, loose ground from THEMIS thermal inertia, cast shadows for any solar time, and radio shadow from the base mast.
  • Best start time, walk replay with live oxygen, a 3D view, a Mars clock (sol, local true solar time, Ls, sunrise and sunset), saved variants, share links, GeoJSON export and a printable briefing.
  • Optional AI assistant that edits the plan through the same actions as the UI.

How it works

  • Terrain: MRO CTX 20 m stereo DTM (1596 x 1512 cells, about 32 x 30 km), with slope from the Horn operator. Where the HiRISE 1 m DTM exists (about a third of the grid), each cell also gets the median slope under a typical step, so boulder fields, dunes and small craters are not smoothed away.
  • Speed: a Tobler-style curve scaled to a suited pace (3 km/h on level ground by default). Grade is signed, so the way out and the way back cost differently.
  • Energy and oxygen: the Santee et al. (2001) metabolic model used by MIT's SEXTANT planner, with Mars gravity of 3.71 m/s², and 20.1 kJ per litre of O2. Loose ground raises walking cost by up to 1.3x, following load-carriage studies (Soule & Goldman 1972, Pandolf et al. 1977).
  • Ground firmness: THEMIS-derived thermal inertia of Jezero (Edwards & Buz 2021).
  • Radiation: 0.64 mSv per day measured by Curiosity RAD (Hassler et al. 2014), shown against NASA's 600 mSv career limit.
  • Mars time: Allison & McEwen (2000), the algorithm behind NASA GISS Mars24.
  • Weather: Perseverance MEDA, with Curiosity REMS for seasonal context.
  • Science targets: placed where Perseverance was localized on the relevant sol (NASA MMGIS), plus Ingenuity's final airfield from its flight log.
  • Heavy calculations (reach fields, auto planner, shadows) run in Web Workers, so the map never freezes.

Benefits and intended impact

Perseverance's discoveries become concrete questions for human exploration: which targets can be reached on foot, at what cost, and with what margin. Every number (pace, mass, tank, slope limit, reserve) is an editable assumption. Mission designers, students and educators can see how each one changes the plan and why straight-line distances mislead on real terrain. The tool is free, open source and needs no account. Terrain, the rover track and weather ship with the app, so the calculations work offline.

Tools and languages

JavaScript, React 19, Vite 8, Leaflet, three.js, zustand and Web Workers. A local tile cache for NASA Trek is written in Rust (axum, reqwest). Data preparation uses Python with rasterio and numpy. The app is hosted on Vercel, with serverless functions for the tile proxy and the AI proxy. The optional assistant uses the OpenAI API.

What is creative

  • Orbital terrain, rover ground truth, weather and radiation are combined into one go/no-go decision for a person, not a rover.
  • Shadow is computed for the Sun at the moment the astronaut reaches each point, not at the start time.
  • The emergency-return analysis finds the single riskiest moment of a walk.
  • The AI assistant can change the plan only through the same 20 actions as the UI. Every number it reports therefore comes from the EVA model and is not made up.

Honest limits

  • Routing runs on a 20 m grid. Rocks smaller than a couple of metres are invisible, and outside the HiRISE coverage only 20 m slopes are known.
  • Ground firmness comes from 100 m thermal inertia, accurate to about 20%. The cost of loose ground for a suited walker on Mars has never been measured, so the factor comes from Earth studies.
  • Radiation is an average dose rate. Solar particle events are not modelled.
  • Dust and atmospheric opacity, suit thermal balance and water use are not modelled.
  • Comms is pure line of sight, with no relays or orbiters.
  • Routes can be planned only inside the CTX terrain model.
  • Speed, energetics and limits are reasoned assumptions from published work (Tobler, Santee et al., Apollo experience), not certified figures for a specific suit. This is a planning aid with open assumptions, not flight rules.

AI disclosure

Claude Code (Anthropic) was used as a coding assistant. The README, the English UI translation and this submission text were written with AI. The demo voiceover is OpenAI gpt-4o-mini-tts, and the video metadata says so. The footage is a plain screen recording. No images were generated. All data is real NASA and USGS data.
